question: How can practiced knowledge leave evidence without a stone monument?
summary: Reaching Aotearoa depended on boats, provisions and learned judgment at sea. Archaeological dates investigate settlement; attributed accounts of teaching and practice explain knowledge that need not take the form of a written chart. Those sources have different purposes, and modern voyaging has its own history.

sections.title: Preparation made sailing possible
sections.text: A canoe needed more than a destination. Taonui describes food taken aboard, water stored in gourds and rain caught during a voyage. Preparing and managing supplies made a continuing journey possible. His account also describes directions held in memory or song and departure bearings judged against land and stars. These are connected tasks: making a seaworthy vessel, provisioning it and learning how to keep a course. They explain practical work without assigning one cargo, crew size or departure point to every ancestral voyage.

sections.title: Keeping direction was practiced judgment
sections.text: The Polynesian Voyaging Society describes modern wayfinding as planning a reference course, tracking movement and finding land near the destination. Its account brings stars, sun and swells together, rather than treating one sign as an infallible instruction. It also names teachers: Mau Piailug of Satawal guided Hōkūleʻa to Tahiti in 1976; Nainoa Thompson learned with him and later navigated voyages. This documented modern practice shows knowledge being taught and used. It does not reproduce a particular medieval journey to Aotearoa.

citations.locator: Modern Methods: teaching history and three components

sections.title: A small trace can test a large date claim
sections.text: Wilmshurst and colleagues investigated an earlier-settlement argument by redating rat bones and comparing gnawed and intact seed cases. Their 2008 study linked introduced-rat presence around 1280 with human arrival. The material, its context and its preparation mattered to the conclusion. A 2022 analysis by Bunbury, Petchey and Bickler incorporated marine and terrestrial dates and distinguished modeled settlement windows for the North and South islands. Research can refine chronology while leaving the exact first landing, named crews and individual experiences unresolved.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 2–3: materials and settlement windows

sections.title: Knowledge continues through people
sections.text: In a 2022 account, Māori researcher Haki Tuaupiki describes examining waiata, proverbs and other narratives in te reo Māori, alongside work with navigator Jack Thatcher. He explains environmental and seasonal knowledge and sharing research at hui and marae. This makes language, teaching and community relationships part of the explanation, beyond a list of stars. A separately dated profile describes Thatcher joining Te Aurere in 1992 and being invited to train as a navigator. These are attributed perspectives and histories, rather than one account speaking for every Pacific community.

deeperReading.title: A chronology depends on its materials and assumptions
deeperReading.text: The 2022 paper does not simply average every published date. It screens contexts and materials, uses calibration curves and compares models. Its North Island 1250–1275 and South Island 1280–1295 windows are highest-probability-density intervals, normally reported at 68%, with model ages rounded to five years. They should not become certain years of departure and arrival. The authors also caution that small rat datasets and traces not directly associated with human activity need careful interpretation. This later analysis and the 2008 rat study are related evidence streams, not identical methods or interchangeable claims.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 2–3: settlement/rat discussion; p. 7: Bayesian Analysis

deeperReading.title: Relationships do not become a simple calendar
deeperReading.text: Te Ara explains how converting generations to years depends on assumptions about their length and selection. A changing calculation need not erase the relationships or meanings carried by a tradition. Tuaupiki’s account instead shows a scholar working through language, scattered records and conversations with a practicing navigator. Only that published account was consulted here: no complete waiata or tribal history has been independently translated. A reader should ask who is speaking, how the knowledge is transmitted and what question an archaeological date can actually answer.

deeperReading.title: Modern success is evidence with its own date
deeperReading.text: The 1976 voyage demonstrates the working possibility of learned wayfinding under documented modern conditions. It is not a medieval crew list or proof of one ancestral route. Thompson’s Hawaiian star compass is a particular teaching system; its maker requires permission for reproduction. No compass is copied here.

evidenceReading.title: Practiced knowledge, a proxy and a dated model
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases of selected publications, not a new translation of an ancestral narrative or a reanalysis of archaeological samples.

items.label: A rat-gnawed seed is a dated material, not a voyage log
items.text: The 2008 study compares dated rat bones and seed cases and infers introduced-rat arrival around 1280.
items.interpretation: The human-arrival inference depends on the relationship between transported rats, deposits and measured ages. The trace does not identify a crew, exact landing, canoe or course; later studies can revise the model.

items.label: A range belongs to a specified model
items.text: The 2022 analysis separates North and South Island settlement windows and normally reports 68% highest-probability-density intervals.
items.interpretation: The intervals are probabilistic estimates from selected material and assumptions. They are neither exact event dates nor a measured travel time between islands. The complete 1250–1300 case remains unchanged.

items.label: A named account makes teaching visible
items.text: Tuaupiki describes researching narratives in te reo Māori, working with Thatcher and sharing knowledge through community meetings.
items.interpretation: This published account supports a particular explanation of practice and transmission. It is not a complete oral corpus, universal community position or permission to reproduce cultural knowledge, and it does not imply approval of this atlas.

familyActivity.title: Match the evidence to the question
steps: Read the supplied capsule together. Write four cards: preparing supplies; practicing navigation; dating a seed; interpreting a model.
Match each card to a question: how can a voyage be sustained; how can direction be judged; when was a material alive; what settlement window does the analysis support?
Separate the approximate medieval settlement window, the 1976 modern voyage and the 2008/2022 study dates. Explain why a paper’s date is not a canoe’s date.
Name a familiar skill learned through practice in your own family or community. What could another person observe, and what would they still need to learn from a teacher?
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: Taonui describes preparing food and water and using remembered stars and swells for navigation. The Polynesian Voyaging Society records Mau Piailug navigating Hōkūleʻa to Tahiti in 1976, and later teaching. A 2008 study used rat bones and gnawed seeds to infer introduced-rat arrival around 1280. A 2022 study modeled different North and South Island settlement windows. Practice, a dated trace, an inference and a modern voyage are different kinds of evidence; none supplies one exact ancestral crew or route. The task uses the supplied text, not an absent image. It does not teach navigation at sea, copy a star compass or reenact a cultural performance. A dated seed informs a chronology only through context and interpretation; a practicing person can explain a working skill without supplying an exact medieval event date.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian or Māori/community approval
review.scope: Five new selected sources, two explicitly retained-and-renewed source scopes, layered explanation, a source-qualified reference and text-supplied family inquiry. The 1250–1300 interval is an estimate for settlement. The 4 November claim review separates the dating evidence from evidence of navigation. No new map, media, annotation, source figure or reconstructed voyage is added.
limitations: Only selected 2008 HTML and selected 2022 PDF text were consulted. Supplementary samples, calibration/code and original excavations were not independently reanalysed; PDF screenshots failed, so no figure pixels are claimed inspected.

The complete ancestral narratives, original waiata, restricted knowledge and full research/recording corpus were not read, translated or performed. Attributed contemporary accounts are not all-Polynesian consensus or community approval.
Modern PVS and Thatcher accounts retain their own periods. No single Great Fleet, exact ancestral course, named medieval crew, universal provisions or precise first landing is recovered.

There is no existing image in this dossier. Te Papa’s Te Aurere page was encountered principally in te reo Māori, and source captions identify modern voyages/photos; no unverified translation, exposure date, reuse licence or new asset is adopted.
PVS expressly requires permission to reproduce Thompson’s Hawaiian star compass. No source compass or geometry is copied or supplied as an ancient Aotearoa chart.
The selected reference does not end voyaging or Māori identity at 1300. Independent historical/community review, real family use, screen-reader/device behavior and physical print remain open.
